source.title: AdAdaGrad: Adaptive Batch Size Schemes for Adaptive Gradient Methods
source.authors: Tim Tsz-Kit Lau; Han Liu; Mladen Kolar

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper, including appendices and references.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares validation accuracy across constant and adaptive batch-size training recipes at fixed sample budgets, using its own image-classification experiments. This is a conceptual test of V5; it does not reproduce the cited large-batch studies' methods.
record.gate_note: The paper's adaptive-batch results and constant-batch comparisons bear on V5. Cited results about other studies are not recorded as rows. Training loss, step counts, batch-size trajectories, and timing are omitted because they are not held-out performance measures for V5.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares held-out accuracy across constant batch sizes at approximately fixed epoch budgets and evaluates adaptive batch schedules against those baselines. These results test V5. It is not an original source for V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that adaptive batch schedules can narrow the large-batch generalization penalty while retaining benefits from larger later-stage batches. They emphasize optimizer and test-parameter dependence, computational overhead, and further work needed for distributed training. They do not establish universal elimination of the penalty.
record.recipe_differences: The study tests adaptive batch-size rules with AdaGrad, AdaGrad-Norm, SGD, and Adam on image classifiers. It does not reproduce the large-batch recipes in the cited studies; experiments use fixed processed-sample budgets and empirically estimated tests.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with optimizer, adaptive test type and parameter, and batch size. The CIFAR-10 CNN evaluates its adaptive test every 10 optimizer iterations; other adaptive experiments evaluate it each iteration until the maximum batch size is reached.

fits_no_version.finding: The CIFAR-10 three-layer CNN table compares adaptive optimizers and test parameters without constant-batch controls; accuracy ranges from 0.40 to 0.58.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive optimizer and batch-test choices affect held-out performance under a fixed sample budget; these comparisons do not isolate a large-batch penalty.

record.peer_reviewed: Statistical Learning and Data Science (venue stated in supplied metadata; the paper text does not specify peer-review status).
record.problems: The authors describe the experiments as demonstrations on smaller models and datasets, not state-of-the-art comparisons. The empirical batch-size tests are approximate implementations, whereas convergence guarantees assume exact population-level tests. Reported validation accuracies have no uncertainty estimates. In some comparisons the tables do not provide matched small-batch baselines for adaptive runs.
record.rows_left_out: The logistic-regression MNIST table reports adaptive-batch outcomes but no constant-batch comparison, so it was omitted. Training loss, steps, average batch size, timing, and figure-only trajectories were omitted because validation accuracy is the relevant held-out measure; aggregate-cost and hyperparameter details appear in Tables 2-13 and Figures 1-15.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Optimizer comparisons under the specified tuning protocols. A shared base learning rate without optimizer-specific tuning does not establish this version.

Language models; longer-training interventions; normalization and regularization changes; batch-specific learning-rate scaling; conventional small-batch references such as 128 or 256; systematic identification of critical batch sizes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.

missing.what: MNIST CNN adaptive SGD results have matched constant-SGD references but were omitted: norm-test eta 0.10/0.25 gives accuracy 0.83/0.88 and average batches 23546/15627; inner-product theta 0.01/0.05 gives 0.80/0.88 and average batches 26078/14593. These improve on full-batch SGD 0.66 while remaining below batch-2048 SGD 0.96, extending the adaptive-mitigation finding beyond AdaGrad.

record.verdict_notes: Budgets are approximately fixed: aggregate tables report small sample-count overshoots. Constant-batch penalties often accompany substantially higher training loss, so these results do not isolate generalization differences at matched training fit. No uncertainty estimates are supplied. The adaptive results support V5's existing mitigation clause; incomplete recovery alone does not challenge its claim that recipe changes can shrink the penalty. V4 and V7 appear in discussion or citations but are not tested under their specified conditions.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep past the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive versus nonadaptive optimizers under the tuning conditions in the version.
Language models; batch-size regimes beyond those in the reported image-classification runs; and comparisons holding optimizer updates, rather than processed samples/epochs, fixed.
Sharpness or other measured network properties tracking the generalization gap.
Removal of memorized training examples and its effect on test accuracy.
